\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:te-family}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my parents and my brothers and sisters in Telugu, choosing the right word for older or younger.}

Name \te{నాన్న} and \te{అమ్మ}, then the four age-graded siblings \te{అన్న} · \te{తమ్ముడు} · \te{అక్క} · \te{చెల్లి}, with \te{చెల్లి} being Telugu's own.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\te{నాన్న} \te{అమ్మ} \te{అన్న} \te{తమ్ముడు} \te{అక్క} \te{చెల్లి}]{\te{నాన్న}, \te{అమ్మ}, and four sibling words — Telugu's own twist}

\label{lesson:TE-C12-kutumbam}



\begin{quote}
Telugu also sorts siblings by relative age. Its words for \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}younger sister,\textquotedblright{} though, go their own way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: Parents — one matches, one is Telugu's own}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నాన్న}} (\emph{nānna}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{father}\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{Telugu's own word}, unlike Tamil/ Kannada's \emph{appā/appa}.
  \item \textbf{\te{అమ్మ}} (\emph{amma}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mother}\textquotedblright{} — matches Tamil/Kannada's \emph{ammā/amma} closely.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Telugu} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{compare Tamil/Kannada} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{అన్న}} (\emph{anna}) & \textbf{older} brother & \emph{aṇṇaṉ/aṇṇa} — near match \\
\textbf{\te{తమ్ముడు}} (\emph{tammuḍu}) & \textbf{younger} brother & \emph{tambi/tamma} — near match \\
\textbf{\te{అక్క}} (\emph{akka}) & \textbf{older} sister & \emph{akkā/akka} — near match \\
\textbf{\te{చెల్లి}} (\emph{celli}) & \textbf{younger} sister & \emph{tangai/tangi} — \textbf{Telugu's own word here} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the \emph{system} — four words, split by relative age rather than just gender — is shared across Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu. But the exact words aren't identical everywhere: Telugu keeps its own \textbf{\te{నాన్న}} for father and \textbf{\te{చెల్లి}} for \textquotedblleft{}younger sister,\textquotedblright{} even while three of the six words line up closely with its cousins.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nānna, amma\textquotedblright{} — father, mother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}anna, tammuḍu\textquotedblright{} — older/younger brother
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akka, celli\textquotedblright{} — older/younger sister — celli is Telugu's own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two Telugu family words are its own, rather than matching Tamil/Kannada? (\textbf{\te{నాన్న}} \emph{nānna}, \textquotedblleft{}father,\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\te{చెల్లి}} \emph{celli}, \textquotedblleft{}younger sister.\textquotedblright{}) Does Telugu still split siblings by age the same way? (\textbf{Yes} — the four-way age-before-gender system is shared across the whole Dravidian family, even where the exact words differ.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\te{◌ా} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S07-vowel-sign-aa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ర} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ా}}
\textbf{\te{◌ా}} — \emph{ā}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ā}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ా} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{నమస్కారం}} \emph{namaskāram} — hello / greetings (namaskāram — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{ధన్యవాదములు}} \emph{dhanyavādamulu} — thank you (dhanyavādamulu — \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{బాగా}} \emph{bāgā} — well, fine — and the reply "\te{నేను} \te{బాగున్నాను}
  \item \textbf{\te{పరవాలేదు}} \emph{paravālēdu} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ా} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ా} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \te{◌ా} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\te{నమస్కారం}  ·  \te{ధన్యవాదములు}  ·  \te{అవును}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \te{◌ా} three times, saying \emph{ā} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \te{◌ా} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \te{◌ా}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ā} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e]{\te{◌ె} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:TE-S115-vowel-sign-e}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \te{ల} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \te{◌ె}}
\textbf{\te{◌ె}} — \emph{e}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{e}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \te{◌ె} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళు}} \emph{veḷḷu} — to go (and \te{వచ్చు}, to come)
  \item \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళి} \te{వస్తాను}} \emph{veḷḷi vastānu} — goodbye (lit. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{తెలుగు} \te{వచ్చు}} \emph{nāku telugu vaccu} — 'I know Telugu'
  \item \textbf{\te{ఒకటి} \te{రెండు} \te{మూడు} \te{నాలుగు} \te{ఐదు}} \emph{okaṭi reṇḍu mūḍu nālugu aidu} — one to five
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \te{◌ె} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \te{◌ె} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}
